Title: Solving combinatorial optimization problems through stochastic Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert dynamical systems
Text:
PHYSICAL REVIEW RESEARCH 7, 013129 (2025)
Solving combinatorial optimization problems through stochastic
Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert dynamical systems
Dairong Chen
,1 Andrew D. Kent
,1 Dries Sels,1,2 and Flaviano Morone
1
1Center for Quantum Phenomena, Department of Physics, New York University, New York, New York 10003, USA
2Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, New York, New York 10010, USA
(Received 28 June 2024; accepted 9 January 2025; published 3 February 2025)
We present a method to approximately solve general instances of combinatorial optimization problems using
the physical dynamics of three-dimensional (3D) rotors obeying Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert dynamics. Conven-
tional techniques to solve discrete optimization problems that use simple continuous relaxation of the objective
function followed by gradient-descent minimization are inherently unable to avoid local optima, thus producing
poor-quality solutions. Our method considers the physical dynamics of macrospins capable of escaping from
local minima, thus facilitating the discovery of high-quality, nearly optimal solutions, as supported by extensive
numerical simulations on a prototypical quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem. Our
method produces solutions that compare favorably with those obtained using state-of-the-art minimization
algorithms (such as simulated annealing) while offering the advantage of being physically realizable by means
of arrays of stochastic magnetic tunnel-junction devices.
DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.7.013129
I. INTRODUCTION
A compelling idea linking physics and discrete mathemat-
ics is to leverage the intrinsic dynamics of real-world physical
systems to solve mathematical optimization problem. The
idea relies on correspondence between the variables of the
mathematical problem and the degrees of freedom of an ana-
log physical system, where the role of the objective function to
be optimized is played by the energy function of the interact-
ing physical system [1–4]. Once this correspondence has been
successfully established, all one has to do is to cool the system
down to zero temperature and wait for it to settle in its ground
state, i.e., the state with minimal energy, which, in turn, repre-
sents the solution to the original optimization problem [5]. In
many cases of practical interest, this is easier said than done
in that during the cooling process the physical system can get
stuck in long-lived metastable states, possibly without ever
reaching the ground state on human-life timescales. In such
situations, the choice of the analog physical system becomes
the crucial point of the entire methodology. Physical systems
that are less prone to getting trapped in the local minima of
the energy function will solve the optimization problem better
than those that get easily stuck.
Many interesting optimization problems are discrete in na-
ture, meaning that the variables involved are represented by
integers, typically taking up only two values, say 0 and 1. A
large body of work has thus exploited the idea of using Ising-
type physical systems to effectively map integer variables
onto binary spins and then use Monte Carlo methods or alike

to simulate the physical dynamics of these analogue Ising

In this article, we present a new energy-minimization
framework to solve combinatorial optimization problems
based on the physical dynamics of real macrospins described
by the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert (LLG) equations. The idea is
to use three-dimensional rotors as the analog physical dynam-
ical system, rather than up-down Ising spins. The rationale
behind our approach is the physical gambit that trajectories
away from the z axis, in particular, those occurring halfway
between the north and south poles of the unit sphere will help
the system to escape from local solutions, thus facilitating the
discovery of the true ground state.
We explain our method in two steps: ﬁrst, we introduce the
stochastic LLG dynamical system and discuss its numerical
implementation; second, we explain how to apply it to a
speciﬁc quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO)
problem, called the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick (SK) model in
statistical physics [7,8], which can be exactly solved in the
thermodynamic limit [9], and show that our method extrapo-
lates to this exact value while performing systematically better
than discrete methods based on Glauber dynamics of Ising
spins [10].

tion presents itself. First, note that at zero temperature the
Glauber dynamics reduces to a greedy one-spin-ﬂip dynam-
ics, where “greedy” means that the dynamics minimizes the
energy along the steepest direction of the energy landscape.
LLG dynamics could be more efﬁcient than Glauber dynamics
because it only dissipates energy slowly. In fact, when the
damping constant is exactly zero [α = 0 in Eq. (5)], the LLG
dynamics conserves the energy and trajectories are conﬁned
to isoenergetic surfaces. In the presence of a small damping
α ≪1, the LLG dynamics follows trajectories that lie close to
the level curves of the energy function. In this respect, LLG
dynamics resembles, albeit is not equivalent to, the “reluctant”
algorithm proposed by Parisi in Ref. [20], that is known to

As in the case of quantum annealing, our method is im-
portant because it offers the possibility of being realized
experimentally in the laboratory by means of arrays of mag-
netic tunnel-junction devices, whose physical dynamics is
governed precisely by the LLG equations. These devices
operate at nanosecond timescales and consume little power.
Interesting future research directions would be to understand
the statistical limits of the robustness of our method across
different choices of the system’s parameters, as well as the in-
clusion of 3-spin interactions to solve 3-SAT problems, which
are of central importance in the vast context that stretches
from artiﬁcial intelligence, to cryptography, and operations
research.

anisotropy, i.e., the control parameter HA. We performed a set

Additionally, high HA renders the system less susceptible to
thermal ﬂuctuations, making the annealing protocol less ef-

to worse performance. Low HA decreases the tendency of the
spins to align along the ˆz axis.
2. Physical insight into the better performance of LLG
dynamics over Glauber dynamics
In this section we suggest and discuss a physical argu-
ment explaining why the Glauber dynamics is more easily
trapped in local minima with high energies and why the
LLG dynamics gives better results by avoiding those traps. A
conclusive explanation would require us to solve analytically
the nonequilibrium LLG dynamics, which is mathematically
quite involved and beyond the scope of this paper. Regardless,
we would like to suggest a heuristic, but compelling, physical
argument to explain the physical reason of why it is easier
to escape from metastable minima in the LLG algorithm. In
order to formulate the argument in the simplest way we need
to introduce a few concepts. First of all, we need to deﬁne
what metastable minima are, which is a nontrivial task in a
general spin model. This difﬁculty is alleviated if we restrict
ourselves to the zero-temperature dynamics of the SK model,
where metastable states can be deﬁned straightforwardly. We
consider a one-spin-ﬂip dynamics deﬁned as follows. Imagine

The results of both greedy and reluctant dynamics are
shown in Fig. 7 and Fig. 8. We ﬁnd that the reluctant dynamics
always ends up in metastable states having lower energy than
those reached by the greedy dynamics. This means that the
greedy dynamics gets trapped in higher-energy metastable
states that the reluctant dynamics avoids by making small
energy-decreasing steps. Here comes the crucial point. We
have already noticed that the greedy dynamics is the zero-
temperature limit of the Glauber dynamics. Next we want to
suggest that our LLG dynamics behaves very similarly to the
reluctant dynamics in the limit of small damping. In fact, as
noted in the main text, when the damping constant is exactly
zero, the LLG dynamics conserves the energy of the system
and the trajectories are therefore conﬁned on isoenergetic
surfaces. When we apply a small damping, the LLG dynamics
will slowly dissipate energy along trajectories which lie close
to the level curves of the energy, precisely as in the reluc-
tant dynamics where only the smallest amount of energy is
dissipated at each step. In other words, the LLG dynamics
evolves the macrospins in such a way as to cause the smallest
energy dissipation and, in doing so, is able to reach metastable
states with lower energy than those reached by the Glauber dy-
namics, in complete analogy with the reluctant versus greedy
scenario.
